audit_metadata.scope: API route security review — 20 route files + 4 server-side library files
audit_metadata.methodology: Manual static analysis for auth bypass, IDOR, cross-tenant access, input validation, SSRF, path traversal, race conditions, sensitive data exposure

findings.title: Plaintext password fallback allows authentication bypass via leaked database
findings.description: verifyPassword() falls back to plaintext comparison (line 134: `return password === stored`) when the stored hash is not scrypt, not ASP.NET Identity, and not an OAuth placeholder. If any user row has an unhashed password (e.g. from seeding, migration, or import), the plaintext password is stored in the database and compared directly. This means a database leak exposes credentials immediately with zero cracking effort.
findings.attack_path: 1. Attacker gains read access to the users table (SQL injection elsewhere, backup leak, misconfigured DB). 2. Identifies rows where `password` is plaintext (no scrypt$ or base64 prefix). 3. Logs in directly with the stored string as the password.

findings.title: Hardcoded fallback JWT secret shared across auth, MFA, and calendar tokens
findings.description: When AUTH_SECRET is not set, three separate modules (auth.ts:17, mfa.ts:12, calendar-feed.ts:17) all fall back to the same hardcoded string 'easy-life-dev-secret-change-in-production'. The auth.ts module throws in production, but mfa.ts and calendar-feed.ts do NOT enforce this check. If any deployment runs without AUTH_SECRET (or if the env var is accidentally unset during a deploy), all JWTs — session tokens, MFA pending tokens, and calendar feed tokens — are signed with a publicly known key. An attacker can forge arbitrary session tokens and gain admin access.
findings.attack_path: 1. Deploy without AUTH_SECRET (the mfa.ts and calendar-feed.ts modules allow it even in production). 2. Forge a session JWT with role='admin' and communityId=null (super admin). 3. Call any admin API with the forged token.

findings.title: Rate limiter uses spoofable X-Forwarded-For header and is in-memory only
findings.description: clientIp() (line 20) trusts the first value in X-Forwarded-For without validation. Attackers can rotate this header to bypass the login rate limit entirely. Additionally, the rate limiter is in-memory (a simple Map), so it resets on every serverless cold start / deploy and provides no cross-instance protection.
findings.attack_path: 1. Send login attempts with a different X-Forwarded-For value each time. 2. The rate limiter sees each request as a unique IP and never triggers the 10-request limit. 3. Brute-force passwords with unlimited speed.

findings.title: Active-community cookie is non-httpOnly, enabling XSS-based tenant hijack for super admins
findings.description: The ACTIVE_COMMUNITY_COOKIE is set with httpOnly: false (line 36). A super admin's community scope is determined by this cookie via resolveScopedCommunityId(). Any XSS vulnerability in the application would allow an attacker to set this cookie to any communityId, causing the super admin's subsequent API calls to operate on a different tenant. This effectively grants cross-tenant data access through cookie manipulation.
findings.attack_path: 1. Find or inject XSS on any page accessible to a super admin. 2. Use document.cookie to set el_active_community to a target communityId. 3. Super admin's next admin API calls (bookings, subscriptions) now scope to the attacker's chosen community.

findings.title: SSRF via Host header injection in calendar feed URL construction
findings.description: The appOrigin() function (lines 16-23) falls back to using the X-Forwarded-Host and X-Forwarded-Proto request headers when NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL is not set. An attacker can set these headers to an attacker-controlled domain. The resulting calendar feed URL (containing a valid JWT token) is then returned to the client. If the attacker tricks a victim into subscribing to the manipulated URL, the JWT token (which has a 730-day lifetime and contains the user's email and communityId) will be sent to the attacker's server on every calendar poll.
findings.attack_path: 1. Call GET /api/member/calendar/sync with X-Forwarded-Host: evil.com. 2. The response contains calendar subscribe URLs pointing to evil.com with a valid 2-year JWT. 3. If the victim clicks the Google/Apple/Outlook subscribe link, their calendar client sends the JWT to evil.com on every refresh.

findings.title: Missing communityId scoping on event invite queries — cross-tenant data exposure
findings.description: The GET handler queries eventInvites and communityEvents by memberEmail only (lines 15-18), without filtering by session.communityId. If a member's email exists in invites across multiple communities, they will see events from communities they are not currently a member of. The subsequent communityEvent lookup (line 24-27) also has no communityId filter.
findings.attack_path: 1. A member who has been invited to events in multiple communities authenticates. 2. The API returns event invites from ALL communities, not just the one in their session. 3. This leaks event titles, dates, locations, host names, and fee information from other tenants.

findings.title: Announcements GET has no communityId null check — potential cross-tenant data leak
findings.description: The GET handler passes session.communityId directly to listAnnouncements() without checking if it's null/undefined first (line 19). If a super admin (who has communityId=null) calls this endpoint, the behavior depends on listAnnouncements(null) — it may return announcements from all communities or none, depending on the query implementation. This is inconsistent with the POST handler which properly checks roles.
findings.attack_path: 1. A super admin calls GET /api/announcements. 2. If listAnnouncements(null) returns all records across tenants, it leaks data. 3. Even if it returns nothing, the inconsistency signals a design flaw.

findings.title: Reactivation action missing cross-tenant check — admin can reactivate any user by email
findings.description: The 'reactivate' action (lines 89-112) checks that the caller is admin/pm/board but only validates that body.email is provided. It does not verify that the target user (body.email) belongs to the same communityId as the caller. An admin of community A could reactivate a user who belongs to community B.
findings.attack_path: 1. Admin of community-A sends POST with action='reactivate' and email of a user in community-B. 2. reactivateMembership() processes the request without community scoping. 3. User in community-B is reactivated by an unauthorized admin.

findings.title: Un-awaited database write in session endpoint (fire-and-forget mutation)
findings.description: Line 47 calls prisma.user.update() with void (fire-and-forget) to clear an avatar URL. If this update fails silently, the user's avatar state becomes inconsistent. More importantly, this pattern can mask database errors and makes the operation non-atomic with the response.
findings.attack_path: No direct attack, but the un-awaited promise means: 1. The response is sent before the DB write completes. 2. If the write fails, no error is logged or handled. 3. Data inconsistency between the response (avatarUrl: null) and the database (still has avatarUrl).

findings.title: Weak minimum password length requirement (6 characters)
findings.description: The change-password endpoint only requires a minimum of 6 characters (line 35). Modern security standards (NIST SP 800-63B) recommend at least 8 characters minimum. There is also no check for password complexity, common passwords, or similarity to the user's email/name.
findings.attack_path: 1. User sets a 6-character password like '123456' or 'qwerty'. 2. Attacker brute-forces or guesses the weak password.

findings.title: Invite code and join URL exposed in API response even when email delivery succeeds
findings.description: Both the success path (line 78-84) and the no-email-configured path (line 46-53) return the community inviteCode and full joinUrl in the JSON response. The invite code is a shared community secret — exposing it in every invite API response increases the risk of it being logged, cached by proxies, or visible in browser dev tools.
findings.attack_path: 1. Any admin/board/pm user calls POST /api/invites/member. 2. The response body contains the community's invite code. 3. If the response is logged by any middleware, proxy, or monitoring tool, the invite code is leaked. 4. Anyone with the invite code can self-register into the community.

findings.title: Local file upload writes to public/uploads with no access control
findings.description: When Azure Blob Storage is not configured, uploaded files are written to the local filesystem under public/uploads/ (lines 142-144, 162-164). This directory is served statically by Next.js, so any uploaded file is publicly accessible without authentication. An attacker who can upload a file (any authenticated user via avatar upload) can serve arbitrary content from the application's domain.
findings.attack_path: 1. Authenticated user uploads a crafted HTML file disguised as an image (if MIME validation is bypassed) or a valid image containing steganographic content. 2. The file is saved to /public/uploads/<random>.ext. 3. The file is publicly accessible at /uploads/<random>.ext with no auth check.

findings.title: Member directory exposes email addresses of all community members
findings.description: The directory endpoint returns email addresses for all members in the community (lines 29-33). While this is needed for invites, it exposes PII (email addresses) to any authenticated member, board, PM, provider, or admin. There is no pagination cursor beyond the take:200 limit, and no rate limiting.
findings.attack_path: 1. Any authenticated user with one of the allowed roles can harvest up to 200 email addresses. 2. These can be used for phishing, spam, or social engineering.

findings.title: Unsafe JSON.parse on sizesJson field without try/catch
findings.description: Line 23 calls JSON.parse(p.sizesJson) without a try/catch. If any product row has malformed JSON in the sizesJson column, the entire endpoint will throw an unhandled exception and return a 500 error, potentially leaking stack traces in development mode.
findings.attack_path: 1. A corrupted or maliciously crafted sizesJson value in the database. 2. GET /api/apparel/products throws an unhandled JSON.parse error. 3. In dev mode, the stack trace may reveal internal file paths and module structure.

findings.title: Maintenance tasks communityId passed as potentially null/undefined
findings.description: The GET handler checks session.role but does not verify session.communityId before passing it to listMaintenanceTasks() (line 18). The POST handler similarly passes session.communityId without null-check (line 49). If communityId is null, the behavior depends on the underlying query — it may return tasks from all communities or fail silently.
findings.attack_path: 1. Super admin (communityId=null) calls GET /api/maintenance-tasks. 2. Depending on query implementation, may see tasks from all communities or get inconsistent results.

findings.title: Notifications endpoint has no communityId scoping
findings.description: The notifications GET and PATCH handlers operate solely on session.email without any communityId scoping. If a user has the same email across multiple communities (or if notifications are not community-scoped in the database), they may see or mark-as-read notifications from other tenants.
findings.attack_path: Cross-tenant notification visibility if the underlying inbox items are not community-scoped.

findings.title: Login rate limit uses IP-only key — shared IPs (NAT, corporate, VPN) affect all users
findings.description: The rate limit key is `login:${clientIp(request)}` (line 24), meaning all users behind the same IP share the same 10-request window. In corporate/university networks, one user's failed attempts can lock out all other users on the same network.
findings.attack_path: 1. Attacker on a shared network deliberately fails 10 login attempts. 2. All legitimate users on the same IP are locked out for 60 seconds. 3. Repeating this creates a persistent denial-of-service for the shared IP.

findings.title: Calendar feed tokens have excessively long lifetime (730 days / 2 years)
findings.description: Calendar feed JWTs are valid for 730 days (line 34). If a token is leaked (URL shared, logged, etc.), it provides unauthenticated access to the user's calendar data for up to 2 years with no revocation mechanism visible in the codebase.
findings.attack_path: 1. Calendar feed URL containing JWT is logged or shared. 2. Attacker has 2-year window to poll the calendar feed. 3. No way to revoke the token short of rotating AUTH_SECRET (which invalidates ALL tokens).

files_with_no_issues.notes: Properly authenticates, validates status input, and the underlying respondBookingInvite() checks invite ownership by email. No significant issues found.
Properly authenticates, checks communityId is present, scopes all queries to session.email and session.communityId. No significant issues found.
Properly authenticates, validates role for POST, checks communityId, validates input fields, uses session.email and session.communityId for scoping. No significant issues found.
Properly authenticates, validates dependent ownership via sponsorEmail check, validates date format. Minor note: PATCH does not enforce communityId but the scope is user-profile, not community data.
Properly authenticates, validates upload via validateMediaUpload(). File is saved with random name via saveUpload(). No significant issues beyond the storage concern (VULN-012).
Properly authenticates and requires isSuperAdmin(). Input validation present. No significant issues found.

Properly authenticates, checks canStaffBookForMembers and canStaffBookInCommunity, uses Zod validation via adminBookingSchema, verifies member exists in the target community. Well-implemented authorization.
Properly authenticates and requires isSuperAdmin(). Validates community exists. Issue with cookie httpOnly is noted in VULN-004.
Minimal wrapper — only creates a Stripe client from env var. No security issues.
Properly handles Twilio credentials from env vars. Phone number normalization is reasonable. No significant issues.

no_middleware_file.note: No middleware.ts file was found in the project. This means there is no server-side middleware enforcing authentication or authorization at the routing layer. All auth checks rely on individual route handlers calling getSession(). If any route forgets this check, it is unauthenticated by default. Consider adding Next.js middleware for defense-in-depth.

top_recommendations: Remove plaintext password fallback in verifyPassword() — require all passwords to be hashed
Enforce AUTH_SECRET presence in production for ALL modules (mfa.ts, calendar-feed.ts), not just auth.ts
Replace in-memory rate limiter with Redis/KV-backed solution and validate X-Forwarded-For against trusted proxy list
Add Next.js middleware.ts for defense-in-depth authentication on all /api/** routes
Add communityId scoping to event invites, notifications, and maintenance task queries
Set ACTIVE_COMMUNITY_COOKIE as httpOnly to prevent XSS-based tenant switching
